As of 230 AM EDT Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: Confidence in afternoon showers and thunderstorms, some 
of which could be strong to severe, remains on track. SPC has nudged 
the Slight Risk (level 2 out of 5) for severe thunderstorms 
northeast to include Essex County NY, and Rutland and Addison 
Counties in Vermont for this afternoon. The areas included in the 
previous Marginal Risk for severe thunderstorms for today has 
remained unchanged. Synoptically, an occluding surface low with 
associated warm front over western New York this morning will lift 
through the region early to mid this afternoon. Showers will be 
possible along the warm front as early as mid to late this morning 
along the southern Greens and St. Lawrence Valley. Water vapor 
depictions upstream into western New York and Pennsylvania show 
decent dry air ahead of a stout boundary of showers in western 
Pennsylvania. This clearing will help our region destabilize this 
afternoon as MLCAPE surges to 1000-1500J/kg, with some pockets of 
1500-2000J/kg across the eastern Adirondacks and Champlain Valley. 
While there will be good instability in the warm sector this 
afternoon as temperatures climb to near 80, with dewpoints in the 
low 60s, deep layer shear will be less than ideal for strong 
organized storms. 20-30knots of bulk 0-6km shear is expected this 
afternoon, which is on the lower side of sufficient shear for severe 
storms; the better shear will be well to our east near the main cold 
front. Regardless, numerous showers and scattered thunderstorms, 
with some isolated storms becoming strong to severe, are 
anticipated, mainly in the 3-8 PM timeframe, moving west to east.

The main risks associated with our storm potential this afternoon 
will be gusty winds, isolated small hail. Although shear is on the 
lower bounds for favorable severe conditions, storms modes look to 
favor some mini bowing segments and multicells which can drive 
strong cold pools and thus isolated gusty winds. Given decent mid 
level lapse rates to 6-7C/km, and good elevated instability in the 
hail growth zone, small hail will be possible within stronger 
updrafts. While the probabilities are low, there is a low risk for 
some isolated rotation within storms this afternoon. As the warm 
front lifts through the region this afternoon, winds in the low 
level will turn more southeasterly, and paired with prevailing 
southwesterly flow aloft, veering flow could lead to an increase in 
low level spin. 0-1km SRH will be low around 100-150 m2/s2, though 
could be enough to lead to some isolated rotation, especially should 
any storms develop along the warm front, and out ahead of the main 
boundary this afternoon. All hazards will be possible this 
afternoon, though the main concerns will be winds in the form of 
straight-lined winds. At this time, a greater risk/more coverage of 
stronger storms is favored south of our region per consensus of both 
the physically-based and machine learning model guidance.

Heavy rain will also be a concern with WPC placing the entire area 
in a Marginal Risk (level 1 out of 4) for a 5% chance of exceeding 
flash flood guidance within 25 miles of an area. Pwats will be 
around 1.5-1.7 inches, the 85th percentile for this time of year, 
with modest warm layer cloud depths around 10,000 ft. While these do 
not favor flash flood potential, the flash flood risk today will be 
driven by conditional training storms. Cells may become aligned to 
the background flow across southern Vermont and lead to a localized 
chance for flash flooding. Probabilities for 2" of rain through 8 AM 
Friday highlight western Rutland County in areas like Fair Haven, 
and Rutland itself in a 20% probability. HREF probabilities denote a 
10% chance for this area to see upwards of 3". These high rainfall 
amounts will be highly conditional on training thunderstorms and 
does still appear unlikely, though there is some better confidence 
than previous forecasts for this area to see some localized flash 
flooding. Have increased rainfall amounts to reflect this in 
southern Vermont to around an inch, to locally 1-2" should a few 
thunderstorms move over the same areas. Interests in southern 
Vermont, should pay close attention to our forecast and radar trends 
this afternoon, as conditions could change quickly.

KEY MESSAGE 2: A cold front will gradually move from west to east early 
Friday spurring some lingering showers across Vermont. Given the 
timing of the frontal passage, instability will be low, so 
anticipating just some light showers. Though should the front slow 
as it nears the VT/NH border, some isolated rumbles of thunder may 
be possible. Showers will taper off Friday early to mid afternoon, 
with clearing skies from west to east. Temperatures will be a few 
degrees cooler than Thursday in the low to mid 70s, with perhaps 
some upper 70s, should the cold front slow as it moves east allowing 
for more diurnal heating in the deeper valleys. Lows Fr
